_note: SYNTHETIC. A fictional five-person automation studio. Not real data.

cards.claim: We moved 12 client projects from hourly billing to fixed-scope pricing, and invoice disputes dropped to zero that quarter.
When our proposals showed three tiers instead of one price, most clients picked the middle option instead of haggling.
Cutting first reply time on a client's support inbox from 9 hours to 40 minutes did more for their reviews than any feature we shipped.
cards.note: One client; reviews are a lagging signal.

cards.claim: Most of our early churn came from clients who never finished onboarding in their first 14 days.
On one client build, a 60-example eval set caught more regressions than moving to a bigger model fixed.
cards.note: Do not generalise to every model or task.

cards.claim: Our automation projects that failed all started with automate everything; the ones that worked started with one inbox.
The automations that lasted were the ones the client's own staff could switch off without calling us.
We hire with a paid one-week trial project, and two of our best hires had weak CVs.
Moving our daily standups to written updates saved the team about 4 hours a week.
Ten customer calls in one week changed our roadmap more than three months of analytics did.
I kept a part-time contract for the first 8 months of the studio, which let us say no to bad-fit clients.
When I stopped working after 10pm for a month, I shipped more, not less.
Captaining a weekend football team taught me more about delegation than any management course.
We tripled revenue in a month with one cold email.
